blocks.x: If I had known that I'd have had this book, Hems, picked out. I didn't know.
Well, listen, you would know no harm to, see things like that, you get excited and you can't do anything.
I get excited. We will walk through the valley, we will walk in pieces, we will walk through the valley with tears of the Lord.
When did they start getting any kind of musical instruments, any horns or pianos or anything out there in Donaldsonville?
In Napoleonville?
In Napoleonville.
Yeah. Well I tell you, I couldn't tell you exactly what I know. After I was a young lady, I used to have music out in Napoleonville, horns and everything else. I was a young lady and then.
They didn't have any fiddlers around the plantation?
Fiddlers in the plantation? No, they had any plantations there.

All right. Let's see. We're talking to Ms. Elmore here right now. So we want to get when you were born and where. Well, I was born in 1902 in St. Mary Parish in a place called Glencoe, Louisiana, out from Franklin. That's near Baldwin or on the other side? Yeah, right near Baldwin. I know Jack Wilman from there. Jack Wilman, yeah. He's from Baldwin. Were you brought up in a church? You must have been. Yes. Which church was that? Methodist, ME. But I'm African Methodist now. You were just ME in those days? Uh-huh. I see. Well, my family were ME in here. But after my mother died, we all moved to Lake Charles, Louisiana. My aunt raised this. And then, well, I went to church a while, but we have to go, have to go with someone else. So she was an AME. And I just went along with her. How old were you when your mother died? Fifteen. I was fourteen. Fourteen. Oh, did we get your exact birth date? Did we get what day of the month you were born? Nineteen october. The month and the date? Oh, no. October 19th. I see. Mm-hmm. Did you hear any music out there, bands or anything? Well, not that I remember. They didn't have any bands, but they did have Cardin and they had organ music at that time. In the church? Uh-huh. Yeah. Did they have any organs outside the church at all? Well, at one home, they were, in case they were plentiful. Mm-hmm. Once in a while you'd go to a home and find one. And they played, it seemed like, with a cypher, you had to turn them, you know? So, uh, we had one at my church there. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. I see. Did they have any other instruments that they played on in your church? No. Just the oil of it. I see. Yeah. Mm-hmm. Some of these churches have all kind of things. Oh, mercy. Nowadays, yes. Nowadays. But in them days, you see, they weren't so plentiful. But, uh, now you can find all kind. And later on, after I grew up, then they had pianists. And then they had, uh, in one church, which I used to visit, I wasn't a member of that, but my aunt was. She, uh, this was a Baptist church. And, like, Baptist church, they had an organ and a, I guess you'd call that a bass. There was great big music, uh, like a violin, but it sit on the floor and they play it. Oh, great big one, huh? Yeah. Mm-hmm. Would they hold it between their legs or would they stand there? No, they just stand there and play it. I see. Well, that's a bass, yeah. Yeah. When did you come to the city? New Orleans. Nineteen, uh, 1938. Nineteen thirty-eight. Nineteen thirty-eight. Uh-huh. So you come here in late years. Yeah. You lived in Lake Charles all the time after you moved from, uh, St. Mary's? Well, no. I, uh, left there and then I lived in Alexandria twelve years. Uh-huh. And after the twelve years I went back to Lake Charles. See, who had a band in Alexandria? John Thompson had a band up there, I believe. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Did you ever hear that band? Uh-huh. What kind of music did he play? Well, they played songs, they had music like, you know, blues, but I, I'm something like her. I never did take to that kind of music. Uh-huh. I never fancied very much. We were. Mostly in the church? Yeah. Would the churches sing different songs in all these different places or did they sing pretty much the same? Well, they mostly sang the same thing. Uh-huh. The same books they were used. So, only after the sheep music came out, well, then you could buy the different music. I thought of something I want to ask her. Let me go back to her. Uh-huh. Did you ever sing what they call Dr. Watts hymns? Yeah. Yeah.
Oh, yeah. I sing Dr. Watts.
Well, what, what are Dr. Watts hymns? What's, what does that mean?
Well, yes, they just, it's the name they call Dr. Watts. Well, it's just a long meter. A long meter is Dr. Watts.
Long meter is Dr. Watts.
Oh, yes, Dr. Watts. That's what they call Dr. Watts.
They have the long and short, doesn't they? Yeah.
Huh?
They have the long and short, short meter, long meter in Dr. Watts. Yeah, sure.
Uh-huh. That's what they call Dr. Watts, the long meter.
Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. The need to charge to keep our head up the core to throw that part. Long meter. I sing it long. You know, you can sing that two ways. I mean, you can sing it two ways.
Uh-huh. Short and long.
You can sing it short, that short and long.
Uh-huh. Well, which one can you sing two ways?
Well, save this pesticide, pulls out a double flood. That's, that's a long and short too.
Can you, can you do it both ways for me? Okay.
Sing it long and short.
Yeah, well, we'd like to hear that. Which one?
Long and short both.
Uh-huh. To hear the difference. Sing it long. What, what, what is it? Sing it, it charged to keep our head.

It charged to keep our head. It charged to keep our head, make all to glorify and never die. Yeing soul to save and fit it for the sky. That's such a short. To serve the presence of thee, my calling to fulfill. Oh, may it all my powers engage to do my master's will. Ah, that's short.
Now, could you sing that same one in Long Mead or would it be different?

It charged to keep our head. Say it. Turn it long. We can turn it off. Phone turn. We can turn it off. We can turn it off. Phone turn. We can turn it off. Phone turn. We can turn it off. We can turn it off. Phone turn. We can turn it off. Phone turn. We can turn it off. Phone turn. I am so too safe and fit it for the sky. Phone turn. Phone turn. Phone turn. Phone turn.

Phone turn. Phone turn. Phone turn. Phone turn. I sang it long, Mead or that last time you said, while the machine was off. So one song can be sung both ways. I see. I got the idea of it now. Would there be any particular reason why you'd sing it long or short? No.

It's just like you would like, you know. It's your choice. If you want to sing it long, you can sing it long. That's mostly Methodist way. Now the Baptist people, they mostly sing it longer than that. . . You can take a long meter.
A long meter you can make it long, you can make it short.
Like Father, I'm special and I'm just here. And I came to Jesus as I was.
I came to Jesus as I was. See, like that.

What do the Baptists do? They sing mostly long meters. They don't sing as the Baptists people do. They sing long meters practically every song they sing. What were some of the ones you named as long meters? Father, take my...

Father, I stretch my hand to thee. And you sing that in two ways. And let's see. Father, I stretch my hand to thee. You sing that in two ways. You sing that in two ways. You sing that in two ways. You sing that in two ways.
No other help I know. If thou withdrew thyself from me. Oh, where shall I go? What did thine only sonny do? Before I drew my breath? What pains would labor to secure my soul from endless death?
Now what about there is a fountain filled with blood? How would you sing that? How does that do you?

You sing that in two ways. With death is different. In filled with blood. Joined from a man well vain. And sinless blood beneath thy blood. And sinless blood beneath thy blood. Lose all the guiltest name. Now you sing the other way.
What's the other way now?

There is a fountain filled with blood. That is a fountain filled with blood. That is a fountain filled with blood. That is a fountain filled with blood. That is a fountain filled with blood. That is a fountain filled with blood. That is a fountain filled with blood. Joined from a man well vain. From heaven's world And sinless blood Beneath that flood And sinless blood Beneath that flood Lose all the guiltest things See, now that's a long meter.
You really stretch it out and you sort of add on to it, huh?

Yeah, you see, you got to hold it up long, you see. Now short meter just like you're talking, you see. There is a fountain filled with blood Drawn from a man well-vain And sinless blood Beneath that flood Lose all the guiltest things See, that's the supplement.
In fact, we call that the Methodist Church. Yeah. Well, what about the Church of God and Christ? How do they sing? Do y'all know? I don't know.

Well, they really do believe they go away with it. They sing the same hymn but I can't catch them. They go too fast for me. They pat their foots and pat their hands and shout and go. Tambourines and guitar and everything.
Don't mind making a joyful noise, then, eh?
I can't catch them. Yes, indeed. Well, I see most of the rest of them but not them. They sound like that.
What's that 110, huh? What, uh? Make a joyful noise, huh? 110, I think.
110, I think.
110 song. A joyful noise.
Did you play music?

I used to fool around with it but I never did play it. I studied across the river from a fellow named Professor Monetta. Oh, I see. I know you, know his pupils. He taught quite a few things. They play in the brass band.
Where did the other fellows used to follow us? Your buddy went to Chicago. Did he ever come back?

Which one? Oh, the clarinet, he was clarinet player. Yeah. No, no, he lives up there now. Yeah. He used to be a radio announcer and be on television. Yeah, uh-huh. But he went up there. Yeah. When you were out as a young boy, you never saw brass bands around Napoleonville much, huh? Did you see any? Not Napoleonville.
I saw them mostly here. Mostly here, huh?
Mostly here.
Not Napoleonville.
What brass bands do you remember from the city here?

Oh, I remember Robichaud. And I remember Robichaud, Jack Carey, and Buddy P.T. and let's see what this other band name is. And he had a band. And Joe Oliver, he had a band. And the most older fellas I knew around here. See, Robichaud, he was an old-timer around here, you know. Where did he play? He was in the Excelsior band. Where did he play? And he was in the Excelsior? Yeah, Excelsior band, a long years ago. And that was out in the street, huh? Mm-hmm. Well, where did he play in the street? You know, when the high parade. I mean, what instrument? The Robichaud? Yeah. Well, Robichaud used to be there, a band. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He used to beat a, well most of the time he'd beat a bass, you know. The bass drum?
The bass drum.
The bass drum. Sometime he'd play instrument, he used to blow a clarinet, he did.
Well I know in the theater he played violin. Yeah, violin. And I never could figure out what he would play in the street.
Yeah.
I know he wouldn't play a violin in the street.
I never saw that. Yeah, bass drum. And sometime he'd blow a clarinet. But in the theater that was all this music, violin.
But I think that's beautiful music violin. Violin, yeah. Mm-hmm. Yeah.
I'm sure.
What did Joe Oliver play? Joe Oliver?
He was a little clarinet. Joe Oliver. He went up to Chicago and died. Oh yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He made some good records.
He sure did.
He used to play in the nightclub when I was 17 when I was up there. You were up there in 1917?
Mm-hmm. That's where I registered to go to the Army in 1917 up there. You were what?

I registered to go to the Army in 1917 up there. And Joe was there when you registered? Mm-hmm. I went up there playing at the same time. Joe Oliver went up there and this boy, Louis Armstrong, he went up there and we all went up the same time. Joe Oliver got to play at one of the biggest nightclub I think was around in that section. Around the state in the 35th and around there in 47. He got to be a famous man. The first time he went up there the fellas were kidding me, you know. The boys coming out there from the south trying to show us how to play music. And Joe got to make records around there and couldn't hear nothing but Joe Oliver. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
Did you ever go to the Dream Land or the Royal Garden or the Lincoln Garden or vacation any other places in Chicago? No.

I used to go to, you know, most places I'd go to right at 35th Street. I don't know what they call that place. I forgot a name what they call it. 35th Street. It's right across from the Mecca building. Mecca flat? Yeah, Mecca flat.
Yeah, Mecca flat.

Yeah, all that's tore down, huh? Mm-hmm. Yeah, all that's tore down. All that's tore down. I was up there in 52. It was a shame. They had a hard upon life when they tore Mecca flat down. Yeah, they sure did. They sure did. Famous place. Yeah, sure.
That was a famous corner, 35th and the State. A lot of things. Yeah, yeah.

Yeah, that building had taken in a whole square, you know, them big squares there, you know. And then you didn't have to go out to get anything, just stay right in the house, bring them for you. Your groceries, your doctor, your drug store, it was always in that square. Yeah, they got it. You know, clothes, any kind of clothes you want, you can just go down there and measure them up and tailors and then send them up for you. That's a wonderful place. It's all tore down. It tore down all the way up to the White Sox Park.
Yeah. Maybe we better let it rest a minute now. Mm-hmm.
It's getting hot. It's getting hot. It's getting so I can't hear good.
I wanted to ask you about back in the old days on the plantation or in Napoleonville, when somebody died, did they bury them right away?

Yeah. They bury them the next day. The next day? They couldn't keep them like they do now. Yeah. After they die the day, they bury them the next day. Well, what would happen? They wake them one night. Would they sing at the wake? Ma'am. Would they sing when they were waking? Yeah. They sing. Oh, they sing. They sing all night. In them country places, trying they sing all night. And go to the bury the next day. They bury them on the plantation. And they bury them six feet in the ground. They bury them on top of the ground like they do here. Six feet in the ground.
Well, would the preacher hold the service then?

Yes. He'd preach over them when they buried them? Yes. Preachers. They can't even hold the service. They sing and pray and then the preacher preaches. They have a society where the society turned out with them. They have their say. That's what they do. They come to. Some of them, they didn't come to no church. They just came from the house to the graveyard. Do you remember the names of any of the societies? They had one out there called the Charity. Loving Charity, I think it was at that time. Loving Charity. But that society had been going for a whole long time. Everybody in that society died open and just let it down. Over a few years ago. Did women belong to the society? Yes. Women and men. They also. Even if they put children in it too. At that time, yeah. They had big societies. That's the only thing they enjoyed out there. And big societies in the country. Well, what would the societies do besides turning out for funerals? That's all just burial. That's all. They didn't ever give picnics or anything like that? Oh yeah, they give picnics in the summertime. That's the only way we can do it. That's all just burial. That's all. They didn't ever give picnics or anything like that? Oh yeah, they give picnics in the summertime. That's the only way we enjoyed ourselves out there with picnics in the summer. And the wintertime would wake all day long, you know. And we used to have winter then. We didn't have no winter now. We can go in here in the summer just like we do. And the winter just like we do in the summer, what I want to say. But at that time, we had winter. We had winter. Snow and ice the whole of the forest. We went out. We didn't go to bed at night. You get up in the morning the trees, we just broke down with ice. Man, we don't have no winter now. We don't have no winter now. We had summer time. We had big picnics. Swinging. Jumping ropes. Playing the ball. A little party. A little dancing. Some of them would be dancing. and all to try that picnic. I remember, sometimes they had music, sometimes they didn't, so I enjoyed the stuff with this. They stayed all so true with that music.
Well, did you all work in the fields in the winter too?
No.
Did you work in the fields in the winter too?

No, no. No, they took a lot. They didn't work in the wintertime. It was cold. What did you do in the winter? I'd stay home to the fire. But they couldn't do nothing when they had all that ice. When they used to have that ice, you know. But after that, we'd plant can. In January and February, they'd plant can. Set the props. January and February, but in December, it would be so cold all that whole month. We couldn't do nothing but stay home to the fire. March. Sometimes it would be so cold in March. It used to be cold in March too sometimes. Did you all tell each other stories when you sat around the fire? Sure, they'd tell stories. It's a child. I know I know. I know about it. It's a child. I know about it. It's a child. I know about it. What would the stories be about that they told?
What would the stories be about the ones that they tell you?
Oh yeah, they tell them.
So what would they be about?
What the story was about?
Mm-hmm. Well, you know. Jack Melanchthon?
Jack and the poor bee, you know. Turtle and the rabbit, and the bear, and the king. Brian, what was the bear? Something goes with the bear. I don't tend to rabbit.
The three little bears?
I've been to the rabbit, going with the cat, with the bear.
The rabbit? You still working in the field, huh?
Yeah.
I think so.

Yeah. I think they worked in the field together. I think so. And about the syrup there? I won't do that organ store. And the old lady in the shoes, I told them in turn, so they know what to do. Oh, lots of stores. I thought I'd just sit down and study them. I had one story. Well, maybe we can come back again. That's the way I was raised, by the fireside. And mother used to tell her story every night before she put us to bed. And then what person put us to bed? I didn't ask to tell her prayers and go to bed and I didn't ask to say a word after she got in the bed. You'd say the devil would get you a prayer if he could go talking. After you see a prayer and go to bed, they didn't ask you to talk. The devil would catch you prayers.
Oh. Maybe you can get together on some of those stories when we come back. Yeah, maybe so. You remember any of them now? No, I don't remember.
I can't tell them, but I remember Jack and the rabbit, I think, who were together. One of them in the house. I believe it was rabbit.

When they would send them home to get them and they were eating up all the syrup. I kind of forgot that myself. The syrup barrel? Yeah, when it was empty, every time they'd send one home, he would eat the syrup. And when the other one got ready to go home, he didn't have anything to eat.
Yeah.
I don't know what kind of one.
Mama used to tell me some kind of story, but I didn't have forgotten that. I was growing up. I was growing up.
Did they talk any French up where you were? No, ma'am. I didn't have no talking French. Creole? I can't imagine.
Everybody was American. No French.
All American? They didn't have no Creole people up there? No Creole people where I lived there.
No.
They were very American folks.
But I know.
Like I know Creole people though. I know. I'm so shaped with Creole people.
I wish you could think of some of those ringarounds. What? Wish you could think of some of those ringarounds.
Wish you could think of some of those ringarounds. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Yeah, it jumps up.

I think of some of them little souls, but we get the same when I retire. I can't think of none of them. I need one. No one inside of all of a sudden in the sun. Oh, no. We just say I'm pretty little souls, though. I can't think of one. Okay, four good ones.
And then we'll turn my face and then we'll turn the soul. Uh-huh.
Let's see. Did anybody ever make up their own songs, or did you all just sing all songs?

I know, but they must have made them up. The people, these old people, they must have made up them songs. They must have made them songs up. And we just got them right from them and we go on and sing them. And we're not.
But you don't remember any particular songs, say, about the Yankees coming or anything like that? No, ma'am.

I can't remember them songs. I can't remember the same as my soul. And I know the plenty of them. It's been so long. Lord, it's been a long time. It's been a long time since I sang a song. It's been 100 years since I sang a song. It's been years and years since I sang a song. Well, did girls and boys play pretty much the same games or? Games. They played.
Did they have baseball then or what kind of ball games?
Baseball. Something ball and nothing was baseball.
Did they call it baseball?

I was a big coach. Young days at any time I used to play baseball. When I was a child, we used to play playgrounds and things in the quarters and all. But I didn't go all day. That's all. When we was young, I used to sing hymns. I was worried about singing the song. I know a pretty hymn. I do know a pretty.
I'm afraid that just about winds it up for the night. We sure do appreciate it. We're going to have to come back again when you get these things together. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.

segments.title: Opening chatter and a hymn fragment
segments.summary: Mrs. Cary is flustered about not having her book ready; a bystander reassures her and she sings a line.

segments.title: Instruments around Napoleonville plantations
segments.summary: Asked when horns and pianos arrived, Mrs. Cary says only that there was music when she was a young lady and no plantation fiddlers.

segments.title: Ms. Elmore's birth, church, organs and moves to Alexandria
segments.summary: Ms. Elmore gives her birth in 1902 at Glencoe, her church upbringing, church organs and bass, moving to Lake Charles, Alexandria and New Orleans in 1938, and John Thompson's band.

segments.title: Dr. Watts hymns: long and short meter
segments.summary: Mrs. Cary explains Dr. Watts hymns are long meter, sings one both short and long, and says the choice is the singer's, Methodists singing shorter than Baptists.

segments.title: Singing hymns two ways: Father I stretch my hand, Fountain filled with blood
segments.summary: Mrs. Cary and the unidentified man demonstrate hymns in long and short versions.

segments.title: Church of God in Christ singing and joyful noise
segments.summary: Asked about Church of God in Christ, the man says they sing the same hymns too fast with tambourines and guitar.

segments.title: Studying with Professor Monetta and brass bands seen in the city
segments.summary: The man says he only fooled with music, studied across the river with Professor Monetta whose pupils played in brass bands, and saw brass bands in New Orleans rather than Napoleonville.

segments.title: Robichaux, Jack Carey and Buddy Petit; what Robichaux played in the street
segments.summary: The man recalls older New Orleans bands, Robichaux in the Excelsior band on bass drum or clarinet and violin in the theater.

segments.title: Joe Oliver and Louis Armstrong in Chicago, 1917
segments.summary: The man recalls Joe Oliver and Armstrong going to Chicago, registering for the Army there in 1917, and Oliver's fame and records.

segments.title: 35th Street and the Mecca flat in Chicago
segments.summary: Talk of Chicago's 35th and State, the Mecca building with all services in one square, and its demolition.

segments.title: Wakes, burial and burial societies on the plantation
segments.summary: Mrs. Cary describes burial the next day, singing at wakes, burial societies like Loving Charity, and summer picnics.

segments.title: Winter weather and fireside life
segments.summary: She describes cold winters, no field work, planting cane in January, and sitting by the fire.

segments.title: Fireside stories: Brer Rabbit and the syrup barrel
segments.summary: Asked about stories told by the fire, she half-recalls rabbit and bear tales, the syrup barrel, and her mother telling stories at bedtime.

segments.title: No French or Creole where she lived
segments.summary: She says everyone was American with no French or Creole speakers, though the man knows Creole people.

segments.title: Ringarounds, made-up songs and forgotten songs
segments.summary: They try to recall ringaround games and songs; she thinks the old people made the songs up but cannot remember them.

segments.title: Children's games, baseball and closing
segments.summary: She recalls playing baseball and hymns as a child; the interviewer ends the session promising to return.
